title: Don't call it an SUV: The Ferrari Purosangue review
gist: A hands-on review of Ferrari's four-seat V12 'FUV' Purosangue: a $393,350-starting, 715hp naturally-aspirated all-wheel-drive vehicle Ferrari insists is not an SUV, priced well above rivals like the Aston Martin DBX and Lamborghini Urus, with the reviewer's loaded test car reaching $576,544.

insights.claim: The Ferrari Purosangue starts at $393,350, but the reviewer's test unit with options priced out at $576,544, showing how quickly Ferrari's customization programs (Atelier, Tailor Made) inflate the transaction price.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A ~47% options uplift on the as-tested price is a concrete data point on Ferrari's per-unit revenue capture beyond base MSRP, relevant to modeling Ferrari's average selling price and margin mix.
insights.quote: Starting at $393,350, a Purosangue is significantly less expensive than the EV Ferrari... our test car’s $576,544 price tag gives you some idea of how quickly the options list can start to add up.

insights.claim: Ferrari prices the Purosangue well above comparably powerful SUV rivals like the Aston Martin DBX and Lamborghini Urus, a deliberate strategy the piece attributes to Maranello's brand positioning.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Confirms Ferrari is pricing on brand scarcity/exclusivity rather than competing on spec-for-spec value versus other ultra-luxury SUVs, supporting a premium-pricing-power thesis for the brand.
insights.quote: It’s also a lot more than you would pay for similarly powerful SUVs from Ferrari’s traditional rivals, like the Aston Martin DBX or Lamborghini Urus, but that’s the way that Maranello likes it.

insights.claim: Ferrari insists on branding the Purosangue an 'FUV' (Ferrari Utility Vehicle) rather than an SUV, despite it being a five-door, all-wheel-drive vehicle with four full seats.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A branding/category-avoidance strategy worth noting for how legacy sports-car marques manage brand dilution risk when entering the SUV/crossover segment that funds their growth.
insights.quote: It’s also probably accurate that Ferrari says the Purosangue is not an SUV but an FUV—a Ferrari Utility Vehicle.

insights.claim: The Purosangue is Ferrari's first true four-seater with proper rear doors and full-size rear bucket seats, evolving from a lineage of occasional-use back seats going back to the 1960s 250 GT 2+2 through the FF and GTC4.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Shows a multi-decade product-line evolution toward practicality, useful context for how far Ferrari has moved from pure two-seat sports cars toward a broader addressable buyer base.
insights.quote: There is an extra pair of doors, rear-hinged ones that provide direct access to the pair of rear bucket seats.
insights.locator: Ferrari followed with its first true four-seater

insights.claim: The Purosangue uses a 6.5L naturally aspirated V12 mounted in a front-mid layout producing 715 hp and 528 lb-ft, paired with an eight-speed dual-clutch transaxle for a near 49:51 front-to-rear weight distribution, at a curb weight of 4,784 lbs.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Confirms Ferrari is still committing to a large naturally-aspirated V12 in its newest four-seat model rather than downsizing to turbo/hybrid, a notable engineering/brand-identity choice as rivals electrify.
insights.quote: that massive 715 hp (533 kW), 528 lb-ft (716 Nm) engine
insights.locator: Underneath that long hood lives a 6.5 L

insights.claim: Combined fuel economy is rated at about 12 mpg (19.6 L/100km), which the reviewer notes makes the battery-electric Ferrari Luce a better daily-driver option on cost/efficiency grounds.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Highlights the fuel-cost/efficiency gap between Ferrari's V12 ICE and upcoming EV lineup, a factor in how Ferrari's own product mix could shift daily-use demand toward the electric Luce over time.
insights.quote: at 12 mpg combined (19.6 L/100 km) that is perhaps a better task for the battery-electric Luce
insights.locator: Painted in lustrous Rosso Portofino paint

insights.claim: The cabin uses a rotating pop-out touchscreen controller for climate and seat settings instead of the capacitive touch controls criticized on the 296, alongside a separate passenger-only infotainment screen that is polarized so the driver cannot see what passengers are viewing.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Signals incremental UX iteration at Ferrari away from the widely-criticized capacitive controls, though the reviewer flags the climate/seat controller as still fiddly while driving.
insights.quote: At least the multifunction steering wheel uses actual physical buttons for most of its controls rather than the near-unusable capacitive touch version that we experienced in the 296.
